name: island

attributes.attribute: a mythological site the Celts saw as liminal, a gateway between this world and the Otherworld
the Isle of Apples, to which the Lady of the Lake guided king Arthur
an island in the western ocean ruled by a beautiful queen, entered only by her will

sources: Kennedy, Patrick. Legendary Fictions of the Irish Celts. (New York: Benjamin Blom, 1969), 219.

Löffler, Christa Maria. The Voyage to the Otherworld Island in Early Irish Literature. Salzburg Studies in English Literature. Salzburg: Institut Für Anglistik und Amerikanistik, Universität Salzburg, 1983.
Ross, Anne, and Michael Cyprien. *A Traveller’s Guide to Celtic Britain*. Harrisburg, Pa.: Historical Times, 1985.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: An island is a mythological site. The Celts saw islands as liminal places. An island was neither quite here nor quite in the Otherworld. It served as a gateway for passing between worlds. Other liminal places shared this quality. They include bogs, stone circles, hills, and springs. They also include built sites such as hillforts and hearths. Celtic tradition holds many mythological islands. Avalon, the Isle of Apples, is one. The lady of the lake guided king Arthur there. The Isle of Women lies in the western ocean. A beautiful queen rules it, and no one may enter without her will. Hy-Brazil appears only once every seven years. Real islands also gather myths. The Isle of the Living in Munster bore no dead. Inisbofin off the Connemara coast showed the mythological white cow every seven years. In Scotland the Hebrides are called the Isle of the Blessed. There budding and harvest come together at once.

okr.objective: Document the island as a liminal mythological site.
key_results: Note the real islands that gather myth, such as the Hebrides.
evidence: Monaghan, P. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore (2008): island entry.
